content_note: All items are ORIGINAL, authored for this project to stay license-clean. They are NOT real LSAT questions. schema ids reference speedrun/taxonomy/lsat_taxonomy.json. This is a small scaffold to exercise the pipeline; expand with a chosen licensed/original source before scoring.

items.stimulus: Employees who use the company's new standing desks report fewer afternoon headaches than those who use ordinary desks. Clearly, standing while working reduces headaches.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.text: Employees chose their own desks, and those prone to headaches avoided standing desks.
Standing desks are more expensive than ordinary desks.
Some employees with ordinary desks also report few headaches.
Afternoon headaches are more common than morning headaches.
Standing improves posture, which employees value.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C is 'too weak': a few headache-free ordinary-desk users is consistent with standing still helping on average. A attacks the causal link itself by offering a selection effect (a reverse-causation / self-selection alternative).

items.stimulus: Anyone who has mastered calculus can solve these puzzles. Maria solved these puzzles, so she has mastered calculus.
items.question: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for solving the puzzles as if it were necessary.
relies on the testimony of a single person.
fails to define what counts as mastering calculus.
assumes without warrant that the puzzles are difficult.
concludes that Maria cannot solve other kinds of puzzles.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: E describes a conclusion the argument never draws. A names the actual error: mastery is sufficient for solving, but the argument treats solving as sufficient for mastery (affirming the consequent).

items.stimulus: The new bridge will reduce commute times, so the city council should approve it: shorter commutes make residents happier.
items.question: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.text: The bridge will not create other problems that outweigh happier residents.
Every resident commutes across the river daily.
The bridge is the cheapest way to shorten commutes.
Residents have asked the council for a new bridge.
Happier residents always re-elect the council.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is 'too strong' — the argument needs some commute benefit, not that everyone commutes daily; negating B does not destroy the argument. A is required: if approving the bridge caused offsetting harms, the recommendation would collapse (negation test).

items.stimulus: Towns that added bike lanes saw retail sales rise. Adding bike lanes must boost local retail.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.text: The towns added bike lanes without making any other economic changes during the period.
Bike lanes are popular with younger residents.
Retail sales also rose in towns without bike lanes.
Some retailers opposed the bike lanes.
Bike lanes reduce car traffic.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C actually weakens (a common cause raising sales everywhere). A strengthens by ruling out an alternative cause, protecting the causal claim.

items.stimulus: The clinic saw more patients this year than last, yet its total revenue fell.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.text: This year the clinic shifted to shorter, lower-priced visits, seeing more patients for less money each.
The clinic hired two additional nurses this year.
Patient satisfaction scores rose this year.
The clinic is open the same hours as last year.
Nearby clinics also saw more patients.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: E is real-world plausible but says nothing about why THIS clinic's revenue fell. A resolves it: more visits at lower price per visit can lower total revenue.

items.stimulus: A magazine asked its readers to mail in whether they exercise daily; 80% said yes. So most people in the country exercise daily.
items.question: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: draws a conclusion about the country from a self-selected group of respondents.
assumes exercising daily is healthy.
reports that 80% of readers responded affirmatively.
fails to specify what counts as exercise.
ignores people who exercise weekly.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C merely restates a premise rather than naming an error. A identifies the sampling flaw: readers who mail in are not representative of the country.

items.stimulus: A larger percentage of Startup A's employees are managers than at giant Corp B. So Startup A has more managers than Corp B.
items.question: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.text: infers a larger absolute number from a larger proportion.
assumes managers are more productive than other staff.
overlooks that Startup A is newer than Corp B.
treats being a manager as the same as being an executive, though it also ignores turnover.
assumes Corp B wants more managers.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D is half-right/half-wrong (an equivocation clause plus an irrelevant turnover clause) and misses the point. A names the percentage-vs-number error directly: a bigger share of a much smaller company can be fewer people.

items.stimulus: Each part of this machine is lightweight, so the whole machine must be lightweight.
items.question: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.text: Every player on the team is excellent, so the team as a whole must be excellent.
This soup is salty, so each ingredient must be salty.
The report is long, so it must be thorough.
Since it rained yesterday, it will rain today.
All cats are animals, so some animals are cats.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is whole-to-part (division), the reverse direction. A matches the stimulus's part-to-whole (composition) error.

items.passage: Historians once treated early cartography as a straightforward record of geographic knowledge. Recent scholarship complicates this view. Maps, these scholars argue, were also instruments of persuasion: a ruler's map might exaggerate contested borders or omit rival settlements entirely. Yet the revisionists sometimes overreach, implying that accuracy was never a mapmaker's goal. The evidence suggests a middle position: cartographers pursued utility and rhetoric together, and the balance shifted with a map's purpose.
items.question: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Early maps served both practical and persuasive purposes, in a balance that depended on their use.
Early maps were primarily tools of political propaganda.
Historians were wrong to study early cartography at all.
Revisionist scholars have corrected every earlier error about maps.
Accuracy was never a goal of early mapmakers.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B captures only the revisionist view the author qualifies; the author endorses the middle position (A), not persuasion as primary.

items.question: The author's attitude toward the revisionist scholarship is best described as

choices.text: partial agreement tempered by a specific reservation.
enthusiastic endorsement.
dismissive rejection.
complete indifference.
confusion about its claims.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The author agrees the old view was too simple but says revisionists 'sometimes overreach' — a reservation, so partial agreement (A), not enthusiasm.

items.question: The reference to a ruler's map exaggerating contested borders functions primarily to

choices.text: illustrate the revisionist claim that maps could be persuasive.
prove that all maps are inaccurate.
introduce the author's own final position.
criticize rulers for dishonesty.
show that early historians were correct.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The example supports the revisionist point being described, not the author's later middle position; C misattributes its function.

items.stimulus: People who sleep less tend to drink more coffee. Therefore, drinking coffee causes sleep loss.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: confuses a possible effect with a cause.
assumes all coffee drinkers sleep poorly.
fails to specify how much coffee is consumed.
relies on a sample of only coffee drinkers.
ignores the health benefits of coffee.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B overstates the conclusion; the error is reversed causation (A): poor sleep may drive coffee use, not the reverse.

items.stimulus: The team started wearing blue socks, then won three games in a row. The blue socks caused the winning streak.
items.question: The argument is flawed because it

choices.text: treats a sequence of events as proof of causation.
assumes the team will keep winning.
does not mention the team's coach.
overlooks that other teams also wear blue.
fails to define what counts as a winning streak.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D is plausible but irrelevant; A names the post hoc error: temporal succession is not causation.

items.stimulus: Only members may use the pool. Jordan used the pool, so Jordan must be a member.
items.question: The reasoning is questionable because it

choices.text: treats a necessary condition for pool use as if it were sufficient to guarantee membership.
assumes the pool is open year-round.
fails to consider non-members who never swim.
confuses sufficient with necessary by inferring pool use from membership.
relies on a single instance.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D describes the reverse inference; the argument goes from pool use to membership, treating necessary-for-use as proof of membership (A).

items.stimulus: If the alarm had sounded, we would have evacuated. The alarm did not sound, so we did not need to evacuate.
items.question: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.text: denies the antecedent and treats that as disproving the consequent.
assumes the alarm always works.
overlooks that evacuation can be warranted for other reasons.
confuses sufficient with necessary conditions.
relies on the testimony of one person.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C adds a plausible real-world caveat but the formal error is denying the antecedent (A): no alarm does not prove no need to evacuate.

items.stimulus: No study has proven that the supplement is harmful, so it is safe to take daily.
items.question: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: treats a lack of evidence as evidence of absence.
assumes all supplements are identical.
fails to recommend a dosage.
overlooks people who take the supplement weekly.
relies on anecdotal reports of benefit.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: E describes a different flaw; A is appeal to ignorance: unproven harm is not proof of safety.

items.stimulus: The law says no one may endanger the public interest. Publishing this article would interest the public, so it must be banned.
items.question: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.text: uses 'interest' in two different senses.
assumes all articles endanger someone.
fails to define 'public'.
overlooks freedom of the press.
relies on a single law.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D raises a policy concern; A identifies equivocation between public welfare and public curiosity.

items.stimulus: This policy is fair because it treats everyone the same, and it treats everyone the same because it is fair.
items.question: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: assumes in the premises what it tries to establish in the conclusion.
fails to define fairness.
overlooks policies that treat people differently.
relies on the opinion of policymakers.
assumes everyone wants equal treatment.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is a vagueness complaint; A names circular reasoning: fairness and equal treatment are used to prove each other.

items.stimulus: You cannot trust Dr. Lee's climate report — she drives a gas-powered car.
items.question: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.text: attacks the person rather than the evidence offered.
assumes all scientists agree on climate.
fails to describe the report's methods.
overlooks electric vehicles.
confuses correlation with causation.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C asks for more detail but does not name the fallacy; A is ad hominem — personal behavior is irrelevant to the report's merits.

items.stimulus: My opponent wants to abolish all roads. Obviously we need some roads, so her transportation plan is absurd.
items.question: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: misrepresents the opposing view to make it easier to attack.
assumes roads are always necessary.
fails to consider rail transport.
relies on emotional language.
overlooks maintenance costs.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: Tone may be heated, but the core error is straw man (A): the opponent likely proposed reducing roads, not abolishing all.

items.stimulus: Either we ban all social media for teens or youth mental health will keep collapsing. We cannot ban all social media, so the collapse is inevitable.
items.question: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.text: presents only two options when others may exist.
assumes social media is the sole cause of mental health problems.
fails to define 'collapse'.
overlooks adults' use of social media.
relies on a single expert.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B may be true but the structural flaw is false dilemma (A): regulation short of a total ban is a third path.

items.stimulus: The museum will exceed last year's attendance because it is hosting a major exhibit.
items.question: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion to follow logically?

choices.text: Nothing else will reduce attendance below last year's level.
Major exhibits always attract more visitors than minor ones.
Last year's attendance was a record.
The exhibit will run for six months.
Some visitors will come more than once.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is too strong and not required; A closes the gap: the exhibit must be enough net of any countervailing factors.

items.stimulus: All interns attend orientation. Some orientation sessions are held online. No online session includes a lab tour.
items.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.text: Some interns attend a session that does not include a lab tour.
All interns attend an online session.
No intern attends a lab tour.
Every orientation includes a lab tour.
Most interns prefer online orientation.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C overreaches; we only know some orientations are online without tours. A follows: those online sessions are attended by interns (all attend orientation) and lack tours.

items.stimulus: After the library extended its hours, evening visits rose sharply while daytime visits stayed flat.
items.question: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.text: The extended hours likely drew visitors who could not come earlier.
Daytime visitors no longer use the library.
The library should close during the day.
Every new visitor came only in the evening.
Extended hours reduced staffing costs.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D is too strong; A is the modest inference that new evening capacity attracted a different crowd.

items.stimulus: Editor: We will not publish op-eds that cite unnamed sources on factual claims, because readers cannot verify them.
items.question: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the editor's decision?

choices.text: Publications should not present as fact what readers cannot check.
All op-eds should include at least two sources.
Unnamed sources are always unreliable.
Editors should publish controversial views.
Readers prefer named sources.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C is too absolute; A matches the verifiability rationale without banning all unnamed sources in every context.

items.stimulus: Critic: The director claims the film is historically accurate because she consulted archivists. But consulting archivists does not guarantee accuracy, since she may have ignored their advice.
items.question: The critic's argument proceeds by

choices.text: showing that a premise does not ensure the stated conclusion.
attacking the director's character.
offering an alternative film that is accurate.
proving the film is inaccurate.
appealing to popular opinion.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The critic does not prove inaccuracy; A describes undermining the link between consultation and guaranteed accuracy.

items.stimulus: If the package arrives today, the lab can start the trial. The trial has not started, so the package did not arrive today.
items.question: Which one of the following exhibits reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.text: If it rains, the game is canceled. The game was canceled, so it must have rained.
Only members may vote. Sam voted, so Sam is a member.
If the gate is locked, we cannot enter. We did not enter, so the gate was locked.
All dogs bark. This animal barks, so it is a dog.
The store is open unless it is a holiday. It is not a holiday, so the store is open.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: A affirms the consequent; the stimulus denies the consequent to infer the antecedent — matched by C.

items.stimulus: Some argue that remote work eliminates mentorship. That worry is overstated. Junior staff in our firm report more frequent check-ins with mentors than before, and retention has improved. Companies should therefore expand remote options rather than retreat from them.
items.question: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.text: Companies should expand remote work options.
Remote work eliminates mentorship.
Junior staff receive more check-ins than before.
The worry about mentorship is true.
Retention has improved in every company.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C is evidence supporting the conclusion; A is the recommendation the argument builds toward.

items.passage: Biologists long classified species mainly by visible traits. Molecular tools later revealed hidden divisions within groups that looked alike. Some researchers resisted the new taxonomy as impractical; others embraced it for conservation planning. The author argues that both views miss the point: classification should serve the question being asked, whether that is evolutionary history or field identification.
items.question: Which one of the following best describes the organization of the passage?

choices.text: A traditional view is described, a challenge is introduced, competing responses are noted, and a pragmatic resolution is offered.
Two scientific theories are compared and the second is rejected.
A problem is stated and three solutions are evaluated in detail.
Historical events are narrated in chronological order.
The author summarizes a single study's methods and results.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The author does not reject molecular taxonomy; A captures the old view → challenge → debate → purpose-based resolution arc.

items.question: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would most likely agree that

choices.text: no single classification system is best for every biological purpose.
visible traits are useless for classification.
conservation planners should ignore molecular data.
researchers who resisted new taxonomy were simply lazy.
field identification and evolutionary history always coincide.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The passage says the two can diverge; A follows from classification serving the question at hand.

items.stimulus: Principle: A policy should not burden a group unless it produces a compensating benefit to society.
items.question: Which situation most clearly violates the principle?

choices.text: A tax on textbooks funds schools but raises costs for low-income students without improving outcomes.
A toll funds road repairs that help commuters.
A subsidy helps farmers and lowers food prices.
A fee funds parks enjoyed by the payers.
A regulation protects workers and raises wages.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B has compensating benefit; A burdens a group without offsetting societal gain.

items.stimulus: The critic argues that the novel fails because its hero never changes; yet the hero's refusal to change is precisely what the author uses to critique society.
items.question: The argument responds by

choices.text: claiming a feature treated as a flaw serves the author's purpose.
denying that the hero exists.
appealing to popular opinion.
asserting all novels must have changing heroes.
attacking the critic personally.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D invents a rule; A reframes the alleged flaw as intentional.

items.stimulus: If the server is down, emails queue. Emails are queuing, so the server is down.
items.question: Which argument has the most similar pattern?

choices.text: If it rains, the game is canceled. The game is canceled, so it rained.
If it rains, streets get wet. Streets are wet, so it rained.
Only members may park here. Sam parked here, so Sam is a member.
All dogs bark. Rex barks, so Rex is a dog.
Either A or B. Not A, so B.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is also affirming the consequent but A matches the conditional structure of the stimulus more directly.

items.stimulus: Since the river flooded twice this decade, and flood walls were never upgraded, the city should invest in levees now.
items.question: The main conclusion is that

choices.text: the city should invest in levees now.
the river flooded twice this decade.
flood walls were never upgraded.
levees always prevent flooding.
the decade is unusually wet.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is a premise; A is the recommendation (conclusion).

items.stimulus: The plan will fail unless costs fall. Costs have not fallen. Therefore the plan will fail.
items.question: The claim that costs have not fallen plays which role?

choices.text: It is a premise supporting the conclusion.
It is the main conclusion.
It is background context with no logical role.
It is an intermediate conclusion.
It contradicts the argument.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D overstates; the statement is a direct premise, not a sub-conclusion.

items.stimulus: Alex: The policy reduced crime. Jordan: Crime fell everywhere this year, so we can't credit the policy.
items.question: Alex and Jordan disagree over whether

choices.text: the policy caused the local crime reduction.
crime fell locally.
crime is measurable.
policies ever work.
Jordan supports the policy.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: Both accept local decline; they dispute causation (A).

items.stimulus: The new curriculum improved test scores, so it should be adopted nationwide.
items.question: Which would be most useful to evaluate the argument?

choices.text: Whether other factors changed in the pilot schools at the same time.
Whether teachers liked the curriculum.
Whether students enjoy school.
Whether textbooks are expensive.
Whether the nation has many schools.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is tangential; A tests whether the curriculum caused the gain.

items.question: It can be inferred that the author would most likely agree that

choices.text: combining morphological and genetic data improves classification.
molecular tools should replace morphology entirely.
resistance to revision was entirely unreasonable.
visible traits are useless for biology.
the debate has been settled permanently.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: Author favors complementarity, not replacement (A).

items.question: The relationship between morphology-based classification and molecular classification is best described as

choices.text: initially sequential, later treated as mutually informative.
entirely unrelated disciplines.
identical in practice.
one disproving the other completely.
competitive with no overlap.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: Passage ends with complementarity; A captures historical then integrative relation.

items.stimulus: The witness saw a red car flee the scene, so the suspect's red car places him at the scene.
items.question: Which strengthens the argument?

choices.text: No other red cars were reported in the area that night.
The suspect owns a red car.
Red cars are common.
The witness wears glasses.
The suspect denies being there.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B could be true but doesn't strengthen identification; A reduces alternative red-car sources.

items.stimulus: Organic foods are healthier because they are natural.
items.question: Which weakens the argument?

choices.text: Many natural substances are harmful and many processed foods are safe.
Organic farming uses more land.
Consumers prefer organic labels.
Some organic foods taste better.
Farmers markets are popular.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D is plausible but irrelevant to health; A attacks the natural=healthy assumption.
